title: Silicosis
subject: Pathology
summary: Silicosis is a progressive fibrotic lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica. It presents with upper‑zone nodules, can progress to massive fibrosis, and markedly raises the risk of tuberculosis.

sections.p: A chronic occupational pneumoconiosis resulting from inhalation of silica particles that induce lung fibrosis. Diagnosis requires compatible exposure history, characteristic radiographic pattern, and exclusion of other causes.
b: History of silica exposure (mining, sandblasting, quarry work).
Chest X‑ray/CT showing upper‑zone small rounded opacities, eggshell calcified hilar nodes.
Spirometry with restrictive pattern (↓FVC, normal or low FEV1/FVC).

sections.p: Silicosis is staged by radiographic extent and functional impairment.
b: Simple silicosis: few nodules, normal or mildly reduced lung volumes.
Complicated silicosis (progressive massive fibrosis): large coalescent masses, severe restriction, hypoxaemia.
International Labour Organization (ILO) classification grades 0–3 for profusion of small opacities.

sections.p: Silica dust is the primary cause; in low‑resource settings other dust exposures may coexist.
b: Crystalline silica from mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone cutting.
Co‑exposure to coal dust (mixed pneumoconiosis).
Concurrent TB or HIV infection that worsens outcomes.

sections.p: Patients develop insidious dyspnoea and cough after years of exposure; physical exam may be subtle early on.
b: Gradual exertional dyspnoea, dry cough.
Fine inspiratory crackles at lung bases in advanced disease.
Clubbing may appear late.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm exposure‑related fibrosis and assess severity.

t.b: Shows pattern of upper‑zone rounded opacities; helps stage disease.
Detects early nodules, distinguishes from TB cavities; unavailable → rely on X‑ray and clinical picture.
Answers whether restriction is present; ↓FVC with normal/high FEV1/FVC supports fibrosis.
Screens for latent TB, crucial because silicosis raises TB risk.
Detects anemia or leukocytosis that may suggest infection; normal results do not rule out disease.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent action.
b: Progressive massive fibrosis → severe hypoxaemia, respiratory failure.
Silico‑tuberculosis: new cough, fever, weight loss.
Lung cancer: hemoptysis, new mass on imaging.
Autoimmune disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis).

sections.p: No disease‑modifying drug; care focuses on exposure cessation, TB prevention, and symptomatic support.
b: Remove patient from silica exposure immediately.
Annual TB screening; start isoniazid preventive therapy if latent TB positive.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.
Bronchodilators for coexistent COPD symptoms; avoid systemic steroids unless acute exacerbation of TB.
Oxygen therapy for resting hypoxaemia (SpO2 < 88%).

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and complications early.
b: Clinical review every 6–12 months with symptom check.
Repeat chest X‑ray every 2 years or sooner if symptoms change.
Spirometry annually.
Enforce workplace dust control, use respirators, and provide health education.

sections.p: Other pneumoconioses and TB can mimic silicosis on imaging.
b: Coal‑worker’s pneumoconiosis – similar nodules but history of coal dust, often lower‑zone predominance.
Asbestosis – linear subpleural fibrosis, lower‑zone predominance, pleural plaques.
Tuberculosis – cavitary lesions, systemic symptoms; sputum microscopy needed.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease; CT is more sensitive.
Spirometry may be near normal in early silicosis; look for diffusion impairment if DLCO available.
Negative TB test does not exclude active disease in immunocompromised patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening dyspnoea or chest pain.
Fever, night sweats, weight loss suggesting TB.

faq.q: Why does silicosis increase TB risk?
faq.a: Silica impairs macrophage function, reducing the lung’s ability to contain Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Fibrosis is permanent; stopping exposure prevents further progression but does not cure existing disease.
Only to exclude TB or malignancy when imaging is ambiguous; not routine for silicosis alone.

exam: What occupational history would raise suspicion for silicosis in a patient with chronic cough? — Identify silica‑related jobs and duration of exposure.
How does the chest X‑ray pattern of silicosis differ from that of asbestosis? — Upper‑zone rounded opacities vs lower‑zone linear fibrosis and pleural plaques.
A patient with known silicosis presents with fever, night sweats, and a new cavitary lesion on X‑ray. What is your next step? — Order sputum for AFB; start empirical TB treatment pending results.
Explain why routine corticosteroids are not recommended in silicosis. — They do not halt fibrosis and increase infection risk, especially TB.
Which preventive measure most reduces future cases of silicosis in a mining community? — Implement effective dust control and provide personal respirators.
Interpret a spirometry showing FVC 58 % predicted, FEV1/FVC 82 %. What does this indicate? — Restrictive pattern consistent with fibrotic lung disease.
How would you differentiate progressive massive fibrosis from simple silicosis on imaging? — Presence of large (>1 cm) coalescent masses in upper zones.
What are the indications for initiating long‑term oxygen therapy in silicosis? — Resting SpO₂ < 88 % or PaO₂ < 55 mmHg.
